newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Opposition slams Yeltsin's hopes on Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Opposition slams Yeltsin's hopes on Belarus.

text.p: The Russian parliament began discussing on Tuesday if it had power to force Boris Yeltsin to quit and opposition figures described the president's call to speed up a merger with neighbouring Belarus as a political ploy.
Gennady Zyuganov, whose Communist Party is the largest single party in the State Duma lower house of parliament, said the suggestion on Belarus was poorly timed.
"I find this suggestion rather strange. As soon as the internal situation in the country gets worse, it becomes acceptable to throw in new ideas," Zyuganov said.
Zyuganov has already said Yeltsin should step down and a communist deputy on Tuesday launched proceedings in the Duma's security committee aimed at forcing him out of office.

The speaker of the lower house, fellow communist Gennady Seleznyov, said the proposal was unlikely to bear fruit. It will, however, be discussed by the Duma's legal department and may be put to parliamentary party groups in a week or so.
Russia's constitution gives the president strong powers and makes impeachment all but impossible. Seleznyov admitted the document was "hazy" on how to get rid of an ailing president.
Yeltsin, incapicated first with heart problems and now with pneumonia, has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since he won a second term in office on July 3.
He is currently being treated in Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital and a Kremlin spokeswoman said doctors would issue a medical bulletin after they meet on Tuesday afternoon.

Doctors have insisted the pneumonia has nothing to do with Yeltsin's heart bypass operation on November 5. But it has been a political blow to the president and creates the risk of another power vacuum in Russia.
Yeltsin's proposals, seen in part as an attempt to divert public attention from his illness, envisage referendums on a merger in both Russia and Belarus.
But Alexander Lebed, ousted Russian security chief, said Yeltsin's initiative was a "political trick".

"The idea itself is a good one, but considering the timing of the announcement, it looks like another attempt to divert Russian society's attention away from vital internal state problems," Lebed told Interfax.
"The Belarussian card, which has become fashionable in recent times, has been played again."

Russia's domestic troubles also extend to the economy, where millions of workers receive wages late or not at all. Teachers across Russia are on strike because they have not been paid and unions say more than three million children are affected.
A delegation from the International Monetary Fund was due to arrive in Moscow on Tuesday for its regular look at the Russian economy, including detailed plans for 1997.
The IMF last year approved a three-year $10 billion loan for Russia but detailed plans must be drawn up each year before the money can be paid out.

Russia won praise from the IMF last year for bringing inflation down, but structural reforms have been slow, stalled in the first half by expensive promises during the presidential election campaign and in the second half by Yeltsin's illness.
But reforms have barely begun in Belarus and the economy there is in a much sorrier state. Economists said Russia could face a hefty bill if the merger with Belarus went ahead.
"I think that Belarus would be looking for pretty sizeable subsidies from the Russians for a while so they would not go under," one Western economist said.
